newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lion to trial world first glowing beer tap.
newsitem.headline: Lion to trial world first glowing beer tap.

text.p: Brewer Lion Nathan is to start trialling the world's first glowing beer tap handles in selected New Zealand pubs within a month, and their manufacturer believes they will turn the beer-drinking world on its head.
"This is the first time in the world that there's been an illuminated tap handle without the aid of wires," Richard Hunter, owner of Christchurch-based Screen Sign Arts, told Reuters on Friday.

Until now, it has not been possible to light beer handles because of the danger of running electric wires close to liquid. But Hunter's unlisted company has married advanced lighting technology with electricity-transmission science developed at the University of Auckland to allow the safe illumination of screen-printed phosphor lamps embossed in the handles.

The so-called "beacon of the bar" is lit by a 24-volt power source transmitted into the handle from inside the tap mounting. Lion marketing director Kevin Kenrick said the glowing handles were an exciting marketing prospect for the Australasian brewer with a lot of potential.
"We are always interested in innovative ways of marketing our brands and this concept is fantastic," he told Reuters.
Brands such as Lion's Light Ice were most likely to be used for the trial and if successful, Kenrick indicated a substantial order could follow, but declined to give details.
"We'll do some testing. A major launch would depend on the results of the trial, but I think the concept has got a lot of potential," he said.
Hunter said he expects to reap multi-million dollar rewards from the glowing beer handles when they take off worldwide.
"The industry has been wanting to have this technology for a long time," he said.

"We've got a lot of enquiries coming out of Australia at the moment and we have people who have started showing the product in America. We expect to be absolutely flat out in a very short space of time."
He said the same beer tap used in New Zealand was also used in Europe, America and in many parts of Asia.
An "intelligent" beer handle was also being developed which could be programmed to flash changing graphics tailored to the customers' promotional needs.
"We can create any effect. The possibilities are endless," Hunter said.
Screen Sign Arts is also combining the technology with unique multi-sequencing progammes to animate large, flat signs, and these too had great potential.
Hunter said British tobacco company Benson and Hedges had placed a NZ$120,000 trial order for the signs and indicated an order in excess of NZ$1 million was likely to follow this year.

"There's a lot of companies that are interested. We believe we're going to be going into production for Keno in New South Wales (Australia), and we believe we're going to be starting to do trials with some pretty large gaming manufacturers, and that's a huge market," he said.
Screen Sign Arts has applied for a world-wide patent on the technology.
